chapters.title: Why Visit China in 2026 and How to Use This Guide

sections.body: I have been traveling to China for over a decade. Married a Chengdu girl. Learned to haggle at Jinli Street before most tourists knew it existed. And I can tell you: 2026 is one of the best times to visit. The infrastructure is incredible, the food is unmatched, and the country is genuinely open to international visitors.
bullets: 240-hour visa-free transit covers major international airports nationwide
China's high-speed rail network is the world's largest - fast, clean, affordable
Mobile payments (Alipay / WeChat Pay) now accept foreign cards
English signage has improved dramatically at airports and major stations
More flight routes and better connectivity than any previous year

sections.body: I'm Joran - American, based in Chengdu, married into a Sichuan family since 2017. I've visited 23 of China's 34 provinces. This guide is everything I wish I had when I first came here.

chapters.title: Visa, Passport and Official Entry Rules

sections.body: This is the most powerful tool for short-stay travelers in 2026.
bullets: Eligible nationalities: 54 countries including USA, Canada, UK, Australia, NZ, France, Germany
Maximum stay: 240 hours (10 days)
Entry ports: Major international airports and select land/hydro crossings
Allowed area: Stay within the province or city of entry
Exit rule: Depart via the same port of entry in most cases
No work permitted under visa-free transit
No extensions: Overstaying results in fines and future entry restrictions
sections.callout: The 240-hour clock starts at midnight of the day you clear immigration, not arrival.

sections.body: Runs alongside the 240-hour option. For Beijing or Shanghai arrivals, check both.

bullets: Valid 90 days from issue; allows 30-day stay (extendable to 60 days)

sections.body: Complete arrival card, submit fingerprints, present passport. Officers may ask: Where are you staying? How long? Answer confidently. Keep your entry stamp.

chapters.title: Best Travel Seasons and Chinese Festivals

sections.body: China is huge. The best time depends entirely on where you are going.
bullets: Best for most of China: Autumn (September to November)
Spring (March to May): Good for south and central regions
Summer (June to August): Crowds, heat, typhoons on coast
Winter (December to February): Cheapest flights, cold north, mild south
Beijing / North China: Sep-Nov cool and clear, Mar-May warm with flowers
Shanghai / East China: Mar-May and Sep-Nov (pleasant temperatures)
Chengdu / Southwest: Mar-May and Sep-Nov (less fog, comfortable)
Guangzhou / South China: Oct-Dec dry; avoid Jun-Sep (typhoons)
Xinjiang / Northwest: May-Oct warm; Winter cold, some roads closed
Yunnan: Oct-Mar dry season; avoid monsoon Jul-Aug
Chinese New Year (Jan/Feb): Country shuts down 7 days. Book 1 month ahead. Hotels 2-3x.
Qingming Festival (Apr 4-6): Tomb-sweeping holiday. Spring travel peak.
Labor Day (May 1-3): Travel peak, especially for domestic tourists.
Dragon Boat Festival (June): 3-day holiday. Zongzi dumplings.
Mid-Autumn Festival (Sep/Oct): Mooncake season. Family gatherings. Travel peak.
National Day Golden Week (Oct 1-7): BIGGEST holiday. Everything books out months ahead.
sections.callout: Avoid Oct 1-7 if you can. Attractions are 5x more crowded and transport is extremely difficult to book.

bullets: Summer: Light breathable clothing, rain jacket, sunscreen, hat
Winter: Warm layers, down jacket, thermal underwear, gloves, hat
Shoulder season: Layers - temperatures vary greatly between morning and afternoon
Universal: Comfortable walking shoes. You will walk a lot.

sections.body: Xian is where East meets West historically. The Terracotta Army is jaw-dropping. The city walls are rideable and the Muslim Quarter is incredible.

sections.body: Chengdu is China at its most livable. The pace is slower than Beijing or Shanghai. People are relaxed. The food is incredible. Pandas are here. And the tea houses in the park are pure magic. Plan 3-5 days minimum.

sections.h: The Best Advice I Can Give You
sections.body: Go in with open eyes and low expectations of comfort. China will challenge you, frustrate you, and occasionally make you furious. And then you will eat something extraordinary, meet someone unexpectedly kind, and see something that stops you in your tracks - and you will come back changed. That is what China does to you. The discomfort is part of it. The food is part of it. The people are part of it. The whole messy, incredible, enormous experience is part of it.

Download your apps before you go. Get a VPN working before you land. Link your Alipay before you need it. Book your Panda Base tickets the night before. Bring comfortable shoes. Learn to say Xie xie. And for the love of all that is good - do not try to see everything. Pick a few places. Go deep. That is how you will actually understand China.
This guide is updated on the 1st of every month with corrections, new openings, and policy changes. The next update (June 2026) will include a full Guilin and Yangshuo Guide. Thank you for reading.
